en: The Sūtra on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha, translated by the Parthian Śramaṇa An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “There are those who serve the Buddha and attain wealth, honor, and favorable circumstances; there are also those who...”
“Regarding those who decline and waste away, failing to find harmony or union—why are they not equal?
I pray that the God among Gods will explain this for us all!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there is one who honors the Buddha, receives the precepts from a master of illumination, maintains single-minded faith without transgression, and practices with diligence, not failing in what has been received; whose physical image [of the Buddha] is kept bright and clear, who performs prostrations morning and evening, reverently lights lamps, makes pure offerings for the sake of peace, does not violate the prohibitions of the Way, and never tires of observing the fasts and precepts, their heart will be filled with joy;
they shall always be protected by the various devas and benevolent spirits, whatever they encounter will be harmonious and auspicious, and all undertakings will increase twofold;
they will be revered by devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and the multitude of people, and in the end, they will surely attain the Way."
These good sons and good daughters are true disciples of the Buddha.
There are those who serve the Buddha but do not encounter a virtuous teacher, nor do they see the scriptural teachings; they merely receive the precepts.
They merely assume the name of observing the precepts, yet they are muddled and lack faith; they violate the monastic rules, wavering between belief and disbelief, their minds filled with hesitation.
Furthermore, they possess no heart of reverence toward the sutras or the images; they neither burn incense, light lamps, nor perform prostrations, constantly harboring doubts.
They harbor anger and revile others with harsh speech, envying the virtuous; they do not observe the six fast days and take life with their own hands.
They show no reverence for the Buddhist scriptures, storing them in worn-out baskets or amidst impure clothing;
or they place them upon the beds of their wives and children in unclean locations.
If one merely hangs it on a wall without any seat or a heart of reverence, it is no different from an ordinary worldly book.

If a person who is ill harbors doubts and lacks faith, they will instead summon shamans to perform divinations and exorcisms, making offerings to heterodox deities. Consequently, the celestial deities will distance themselves and fail to provide protection; malevolent spirits will advance daily, and evil ghosts will block the gates, causing decline and exhaustion so that whatever one undertakes meets with failure.

Some have come from evil paths due to their past conduct and are sinners in the present life; they are not disciples of the Buddha and, upon death, shall enter the hells to undergo torture and punishment.

Due to these transgressions, one experiences decline and exhaustion in the present life, and subsequently undergoes calamity; after death, one proceeds toward the evil realms, undergoing successive torments that are beyond description—this is all because of the accumulation of evil and unwholesome conduct.

"Deluded and blind are the fools; they do not contemplate the destination of the spirit through the causes and conditions of past deeds, nor the fundamental origins of retribution, yet they claim that serving the Buddha has led to this decline and ruin."

Not only do they lack the merit of their past lives, but they harbor resentment toward Heaven and Earth, and blame the sages and fault Heaven. The delusions of worldly people reach such a state that they fail to understand.

Those who fail to understand have unsettled minds and lack steadfastness; they lose the proper way in both advancing and retreating, violating and betraying the Buddha’s grace without any sense of reciprocity. Consequently, they become entangled and bound by the three miserable realms, creating their own misfortunes and blessings.

The conditions for sinful consciousness are the very roots from which they spring; one must not fail to be cautious. The ten evil deeds are enemies, while the ten wholesome deeds are steadfast friends. To settle the spirit and attain the Way—all arises from the wholesome.
Virtue is a great armor, by which one does not fear weapons;
virtue is a great ship, by which one may cross over waters.
One who is able to maintain faith finds peace and harmony within their home; blessings and rewards come naturally, proceeding from good to better, for they are not bestowed by a deity.
"If they now lack faith again, it will become even more severe from this point forward!
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!..."
Good and evil pursue a person like a shadow follows a form; they cannot be separated.
The matters of transgression and merit are likewise so; do not harbor doubt, lest you fall into the evil realms yourself!
"Sin and merit are distinct; those who believe with clarity and without delusion will always abide in peace wherever they are.
The Buddha’s words are most sincere; they never deceive anyone.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
“The Buddha’s word is never twofold; a Buddha is difficult to encounter in this world, and the Dharma of the sutras is difficult to hear.

You possess merit from past lives and have now been able to attend upon the Buddha; you should therefore contemplate repaying his kindness by proclaiming the teachings of the Dharma, manifesting them to the people, and acting as a field of merit for them.”
"Those with faith shall find firm root; in future lives they shall have no sorrow.
Ānanda received these instructions and propagated them far and wide.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a person does not kill with their own hands, is it because they do not kill with their own hands that they are without fault?
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
To teach others to kill is more serious than to kill on one's own.
Why is this? It may be that the person is a slave, a child, or a lowly person who does not understand the nature of sin and merit.

Or, if one is coerced by local officials and does not act of one's own volition, although the offense may be incurred, the intent differs from that of the instigator, and thus there is a difference in the gravity of the punishment.
One who incites another to kill does so with full knowledge and deliberate intent; harboring inner folly and evil, they reach out their hand to harm a living being without a heart of compassion.
To deceive the Triple Gem and betray the Natural Spirit, thereby injuring life and truncating destiny—there is no crime greater than this!
Retaliating against one’s enemies leads to suffering endured life after life without end.
In this present life, there is no peace, and one repeatedly encounters calamities and misfortunes;

upon death, one enters hell. Only after emerging from that human form will one fall among the animals, where one is slaughtered and butchered by humans. For trillions of kalpas across the three miserable realms and eight difficulties, one provides flesh for others with no time of release, enduring physical torment while eating grass and drinking from springs.

In this present world, there currently exist such species of beasts; all of them resulted from their previous lives as humans when they were violent, rebellious, and unprincipled, secretly harming and injuring living beings, and through their lack of faith, they reached this state.
"Life after life they act as enemies, returning harm for harm; though their spirits are the same, their forms differ, yet their transgressions are as profound as this.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying, "If people of the world or the disciples harbor evil intentions toward their teachers or those of moral virtue, what is their transgression?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"As for those who are human, they ought to love and delight in the virtues of others and must not be envious of them.
If a person harbors ill will toward one who possesses the Way and its Virtue or toward a virtuous teacher, this is no different from harboring ill will toward the Buddha."
"It would be better to draw a ten-thousand-stone crossbow and shoot oneself than to harbor an evil intent toward him.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
"Would it not be painful to shoot oneself?
Ānanda replied, "It would be extremely painful, extremely painful!"
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
"If a person harbors an evil intent toward one who possesses virtue and morality, or toward their own good teacher, the pain is more intense than being struck by a bowshot in the body."

As a disciple, one must not treat one’s teacher with contempt or harbor ill will toward those who possess virtue; one should regard them as a Buddha, never being disdainful or envious, and should rejoice in their goodness on their behalf.
Those who possess the virtue of precepts move the various devas; among devas, nāgas, and spirits, there are none who do not revere them.
It would be better to cast one's body into fire or have one's flesh cut by a sharp sword than to ever harbor jealousy toward the goodness of others.
"The offense is no small matter; be careful! Be careful!
Ānanda spoke again to the Buddha, saying:

"One who acts as a teacher may rebuke or restrain their disciples; if they do not follow the Way because of a minor transgression, and that [reproach] subsequently leads to a great [offense], can the teacher be considered without fault?"
The Buddha said: "It must not be! It must not be!"
Regarding the relationship between teacher and disciple, their mutual resonance is spontaneous; they should treat one another with profound courtesy and regard each other as themselves.

One should correct others through principle and instruct them through the Way, never imposing upon others what one does not practice oneself. One should propagate and honor ritual and discipline so that resentment and litigation do not arise;
the disciple should likewise act in this manner.

In these two matters, let there be sincerity: the teacher should act as a teacher, and the disciple should act as a disciple. Do not slander one another, harbor malice, or breed resentment; do not turn small matters into great ones, lest you burn yourselves from within.
As a disciple, you should be filial and obedient toward your virtuous teacher; be careful never to harbor ill will toward him.

To harbor ill will toward one's teacher is no different from harboring ill will toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha of bhikṣus, or one’s own parents; such a person is not sheltered by heaven nor supported by earth.
Observe those wicked people of the final age who are neither loyal nor filial, devoid of benevolence and righteousness, and who do not follow the way of humanity.

Among the four types of bhikṣus in this demonic age, they think only of the faults of others while failing to restrain their own evils; they envy the worthy and are jealous of the good, seeking to obstruct and ruin one another.

They do not contemplate practicing virtue, but are instead arrogant and envious of the worthy; being unable to practice it themselves, they further disparage and destroy others, severing their resolve for the Path and preventing them from practicing it.

Those who are greedy and devoted to worldly affairs, who seek much profit and toil, lose themselves by amassing wealth; they value riches and despise the Way, falling after death into the great hells of the evil destinies—among hungry ghosts and animals—which they ought not yet to have reached.
What do you seek in this world? You should contemplate repaying the Buddha’s kindness by upholding the sutras and the precepts, and leading one another along the Way.
One must not fail to study the Way; one must not fail to read the sutras; and one must not fail to practice the good.

Practice virtue and disseminate goodness to deliver the spirit from suffering and transcend birth and death; do not treat the worthy with arrogance, do not slander the good, and do not use a minor transgression to prove one guilty of a great crime.
"To act contrary to the Dharma and violate reason is a crime of no small magnitude; since there is evidence for both sin and merit, how can one not be cautious?
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the final age, disciples will arise through the conditions of dependent origination. Regarding the affairs of managing a household and the burdens of body and speech, what should they do?"
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!

There are those who receive the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts and faithfully practice them, being filial and reverent, cautious and prudent, and respectfully taking refuge in the Three Honored Ones; they nurture their parents with utmost loyalty, are careful and virtuous both internally and externally, and ensure that mind and speech correspond. Such persons may engage in worldly affairs, yet they cannot harbor worldly intentions.
Ānanda said: "World-Honored One, what are worldly matters and worldly intentions?
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:

"As disciples of the Buddha, you may engage in trade and business for a livelihood, using level measures and straight rulers; you must not deceive others, conducting your affairs with reason and without contravening the natural principles of the divine spirits."
Matters such as funerals, moving house, marriage, and so forth, are worldly affairs.

Regarding "worldly intentions," as a disciple of the Buddha, one must not practice divination, summon spirits, use talismans or incantations, perform rites to suppress anomalies, conduct sacrifices, or offer petitions for deliverance; nor should one select auspicious days or favorable times.

One who has received the Five Precepts of the Buddha is a person of merit; whatever they undertake, they should inform the Triple Gem, for the profound penetration of the Buddha knows nothing too subtle.
For one whose virtue lies in the precepts, the protection of the Way is powerful; they can employ the various devas, nāgas, and spirits, none of whom fail to show reverent submission.
When the precepts are honored, one is dignified, and there is no place one goes that is not auspicious; how could there be any taboos or inauspiciousness?
"The Way encompasses and covers all, embracing heaven and earth in its vastness; yet those who do not understand it create their own obstructions for themselves.
Good and evil arise from the human mind; fortune and misfortune depend on man, following him like a shadow pursuing a form or an echo responding to a sound."
The virtue of their preceptual conduct accords with nature; they are protected by the various devas, and their vows never fail. They move the ten directions and share in the merit of the heavens;
their achievements are so lofty that all the sages praise them, for they are difficult to measure.

"The wise man who understands destiny remains upright throughout his life and does not fall into evil; by practicing in accordance with the Buddha's teachings, he may attain the Way that transcends the world.
Having heard the Buddha’s words, Ānanda adjusted his monastic robe, prostrated himself with his head to the ground, and said:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"

We are fortunate to have encountered the Tathāgata, whose universal kindness and compassion are great; he takes pity on all beings, acts as a field of merit for us, and enables us to be liberated from suffering.
The Buddha’s words are those of the Most Truthful, yet those who believe in them are few; this world abounds in evil, and sentient beings curse one another—how truly lamentable!
If there are those with faith, whether one or two, how can it be that the world is so wicked and degenerate to such an extent?
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, although the scriptures and Dharma shall remain, there will be none who believe them; thus they will gradually decline and perish!
Alas! How painful!
"On whom shall we rely?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will not enter *nirvāṇa* for the sake of the common people.
Thereupon, Ānanda offered this admonition in verse:
"The Buddha is the protector of the three realms; his grace is vast and his compassion great.
For the sake of all beings, we pray that you do not yet enter parinirvāṇa.
Those who encounter the Dharma are few; they are blind and blind, unable to distinguish the true."
How painful it is for those who do not understand; their transgressions are so profound as this!
Those with past merit who encounter the Dharma—whether one or two of them—will find the sutras and teachings gradually decline; what shall they rely upon then?
The Buddha’s grace is not small; yet because of sentient beings’ transgressions, The Dharma drum resounds through the three thousandfold world—how could they not hear it?
In this turbid age, many are evil people; They fall back into their own inverted views.
Flattering and slandering the Sage, they use crooked flattery to destroy the True and Right.
They do not believe that there is a Buddha in the world, claiming that the Buddha is not the Great Way;
asserting that he is a man and not a non-man, they create for themselves the root of manifold sins.
When life ends, one goes to the Avīci Hell; swords and blades sever the body.
Those who delighted in killing devour ghosts, while boiling cauldrons surge within them.
The lewd embrace the copper pillar, as great fires burn them together.
Those who slander pure and noble sages shall have their tongues pulled out with iron tongs.
Those who are intoxicated by disorderly wine and lack propriety will be deluded and lose the way of humanity;
upon death, they enter hell, where molten copper is poured into their mouths.
Encountering manifold calamities and hardships, with agonizing pain beyond description,
even if one returns to life as a human, it will be among the lowly and the impoverished.
By not killing, one attains long life, free from illness and always robust and strong.
By not stealing, one becomes greatly wealthy in the future, with wealth and treasures always overflowing;
by not committing sexual misconduct, one’s fragrance remains pure, the body is fresh and fragrant,
one’s radiance is ever resplendent, and one shall become a great king above.
Sincere and free from deceit, one is honored and supported by the multitude;
sober and clear-minded even after drinking, one is revered for virtue and wisdom.
With five blessings surpassing those of the mundane world, such a person is a peer among devas and humans.
The merit produced is hundreds of millions of times greater; the True Dharma is exceedingly clear.
Yet in the final age, all those evil people will lack faith and harbor much doubt;
being ignorant and unable to distinguish the Way, their sins deepen and they shall fall further into darkness!
Having obscured the sages and reviled the Perfectly Awakened One, one dies and enters the Great Iron City;
with the consciousness-spirit dwelling within, one bears an iron wheel upon the head.
Seeking death but unable to die, in an instant one’s form is transformed.
Spears and halberds poison and pierce one another; bodies are constantly mangled and severed.
How can the world be thus? Turning one's back on the Right, one believes in ghosts and spirits;
one delights in divination and inquiry, while performing sacrifices that are cruel and unkind.
Upon death, one falls into the eighteen hells, passing through the Black Rope Prison;
with the eight difficulties as the foremost of realms, it is difficult to regain a human body.
Even when one does obtain a human form, there are those who are barbarians and devoid of moral principle.
Foolish and witless, devoid of any opening for wisdom; Lame, crippled, mute, and unable to speak;
Obscured and failing to comprehend matters, Bound and constrained by mutual evil;
Gathering together in shifting throngs, Taking on the forms of birds, beasts, and domestic animals.
Being slaughtered and dismembered by others, With skin flayed and their throats exposed,
they return to settle old grudges, Giving back their flesh to those from whom it was taken.
Falling into evil realms through unrighteousness, Seeking liberation is exceedingly difficult.
Human existence is difficult to obtain, and the Buddha’s scriptures are difficult to hear.
The World-Honored One is the Protector of the Multitudes; all within the three realms receive his grace.
He spreads the moving Dharma of ambrosia, causing all people to practice it universally.
Alas! Having attained wisdom, out of compassion for all living beings, he opens and reveals the path; the wise immediately cross over suffering.
The person of merit moves toward [the goal]; seeing the Truth, they train so as not to be born again.
I take refuge in the Great Protector Field, planting seeds in the ground of immortality.
There is no kindness greater than that of the Buddha, who turns the Wheel of Dharma for the world’s benefit;
may all people obtain the drink of nectar.
"The boat of wisdom reaches the other shore; The Dharma-bell leads across the great chiliocosm.
Self and other are non-dual; I vow for the unsurpassed truth.

After Ānanda had recited these verses, the entire assembly simultaneously attained faith and understanding. They all resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, donning the great armor of *saṃnāha* (the monastic vows) and the intent of the nectar of immortality. Their fragrance perfumed the three thousandfold world-system, and through this they were delivered. He revealed the stages of the Path and acted as a bridge for them.

The king, his ministers and subjects, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, rejoiced upon hearing the sutra; Ānanda, however, spoke with both grief and trepidation. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and paid homage to Ānanda, then received his instructions and departed.
The Sutra on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha Asked by Ānanda.
